chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man has a right against me, and he denies it to me. Then he entrusts me with wealth. Is it for me to take my wealth from him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No. This is betrayal.'
ai.seo_question: Can a debtor take money from a creditor's entrusted wealth if the creditor denies the debt was paid?
ai.summary: In this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), the distinction is made between a legal claim and physical possession; even if the debtor is owed money, unilaterally seizing funds from wealth specifically entrusted (wadi'ah) to him constitutes *khiyanah* (betrayal of trust) rather than lawful recovery. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on preserving the sanctity of the trust relationship (*amanah*) separate from the debt obligation, ensuring that one does not violate the terms of the deposit to settle a separate claim. The ruling underscores that *khiyanah* here refers to the breach of the specific custodial agreement, serving as a practical guide for maintaining ethical financial conduct in commercial transactions.
